facts.text: The red-tailed hawk is a bird of prey and one of the most common hawks in North America.

Though lost habitat has thinned its numbers, the singer is still very common.

tagline.text: Loud twichety song, soft jip call, and a nest down low.

facts.text: The northern pygmy owl is a small owl native to western North America.

Northern pygmy owls are purportedly "sit-and-wait" predators, though they also hunt somewhat actively, moving from perch to perch with short flights, and pursuing prey at all levels of forest structure.
They usually nest in a tree cavity and will often use old woodpecker holes.
As small birds of prey, northern pygmy owls are vulnerable to many human threats.
In Oregon and Washington they are known to nest and forage in the center of dense, continuous forests, near streams.
They swoop down on prey; they may also catch insects in flight.
The female lays 2–7 eggs, typically 4–6.
One of the biggest threats to their population is the loss of mature forests and woodlands to high-frequency, high severity wildfires.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 30 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 61 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cavity.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: In the dense, unbroken forests of Oregon and Washington, near the streams, a small hunter keeps watch.
It sits and waits, they say, then hops from perch to perch on short flights, chasing prey at every level of the woods.
It swoops down on prey and may catch insects in midair.
It nests in a tree hollow, often an old woodpecker hole.
Among its greatest dangers are fierce, frequent wildfires that burn away old forests.

tagline.text: It waits on the branch, then swoops.

facts.text: The house finch is a North American bird in the finch family.
House finches forage on the ground or in vegetation normally.
Nests are made in cavities, including openings in buildings, hanging plants, and other cup-shaped outdoor decorations.
Analyses of nest records from house finches in California spanning more than a century found that egg‐laying occurred significantly earlier in warmer springs.
The mite Pellonyssus reedi is often found on house finch nestlings, particularly for nests later in the season.
Male coloration varies in intensity with the seasons and is derived from the berries and fruits in its diet.
They primarily eat grains, seeds and berries, being voracious consumers of weed seeds such as nettle and dandelion; included are incidental small insects such as aphids.
Sometimes nests abandoned by other birds are used.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 24 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 21 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Look for the house finch's nest in an opening in a building, a hanging plant, or a cup-shaped outdoor decoration.
Sometimes it simply moves into a nest another bird left behind.
Its feast is grains, seeds and berries, and it greedily gobbles weed seeds like nettle and dandelion, with a stray aphid now and then.
The male wears his meals: his color comes from the berries and fruits he eats, and it deepens and fades with the seasons.

tagline.text: A finch that wears the berries it eats.

facts.text: The purple finch is a bird in the finch family, Fringillidae.
They mainly eat seeds, berries, and insects.
The purple finch prefers nesting in lowland coniferous and mixed forests, avoiding more heavily populated urban areas, but sometimes is found in rural areas.
The continuous song has an up-and-down cadence of various notes.
The female usually builds a nest on horizontal branches of coniferous trees, away from the trunk, but occasionally in tree forks.
Nesting females have their own songs.
It breeds in the northern United States, southern Canada, and the west coast of North America.
Their breeding habitat is coniferous and mixed forest in Canada and the northeastern United States, as well as various wooded areas along the U.S. Pacific coast.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 25 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 23 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in forest.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Out on a level branch of a cone-bearing tree, away from the trunk, the female most often builds her nest.
Now and then she chooses a fork in the tree instead.
Her kind prefers to nest in lowland forests of conifers and mixed trees, shunning crowded towns, though they are sometimes found in the countryside.
While she nests, she sings songs all her own.
And the bird's long, unbroken song rises and falls over many different notes.

tagline.text: She builds out on the level bough, singing her own song.

facts.text: The bald eagle is a bird of prey found in North America.
It reaches speeds of 56–70 km/h when gliding and flapping, and about 48 km/h while carrying fish.
Bald eagles have high mate fidelity and generally mate for life.
The Pawnee consider eagles as symbols of fertility because their nests are built high off the ground and because they fiercely protect their young.
In March 2024, bald eagles were found nesting in Toronto for the first time.
Bald eagles, like many birds of prey, were especially affected by DDT due to biomagnification.
The highly developed talon of the hind toe is used to pierce the vital areas of prey while it is held immobile by the front toes.
It is found near large bodies of open water with an abundant food supply and old-growth trees for nesting.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 209 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 4.7 kg.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a half cup.
It lays 1 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Where open water lies wide and old trees stand tall, the bald eagle of North America makes its home.
Its front toes hold the prey still while the great hind talon pierces its vital places.
Even carrying fish, it flies at about 48 kilometres an hour.
A pair, once joined, most often stays together for life.
The Pawnee see eagles as signs of fertility, for their nests sit high off the ground and they fiercely guard their young.

tagline.text: Lord of open water, true to its mate for life.

facts.text: The barn swallow is the most widespread species of swallow in the world, occurring on all continents, with vagrants reported even in Antarctica.
The barn swallow is a bird of open country that normally nests in man-made structures and consequently has spread with human expansion.
The barn swallow is similar in its habits to other aerial insectivores, including other swallow species and the unrelated swifts.
The male barn swallow returns to the breeding grounds before the females and selects a nest site, which is then advertised to females with a circling flight and song.
Males sing to defend small territories and to attract mates.
The barn swallow is an attractive bird that feeds on flying insects and has therefore been tolerated by humans when it shares their buildings for nesting.

The same individuals often breed at the same site year after year, although settlement choices have been experimentally shown to be predicted by nest availability rather than any characteristics of available mates.
Hot dry summers will reduce the availability of insect food for chicks.
Its wingspan is about 32 cm.
It weighs about 18 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in towns, farms and other places people have changed.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: The male swallow returns to the breeding grounds before the females and picks a nest site.
Then he circles above it, singing, to show it to the females.
A bird of open country, he nests in what people build, and so he has spread as people spread.
People let him share their buildings, for he eats flying insects.
Year after year, the same birds often return to the same place, drawn more by an open nest than a mate.

tagline.text: He picks the nest, then circles it in song.

facts.text: The harlequin duck is a small sea duck.
They eat molluscs, crustaceans and insects.
Young ducks begin courtship in their first winter, females will find success by the second year, yet the males will rarely form a persistent bond before their fourth winter.
The nest is usually located in a well-concealed location on the ground near a stream.
Their breeding habitat is cold fast moving streams in northwestern and northeastern North America, Greenland, Iceland and eastern Russia.
Harlequins have smooth, densely packed feathers that trap a lot of air within them.
Harlequin ducks adhere to a monogamous mating system, during their winter mating season will form multi-year pair bonds, though the males rarely participate in paternal care.
Adult breeding males have a colorful and complex plumage pattern.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 68 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 562 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in the open sea.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 9 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Where cold streams run fast, from Greenland and Iceland to eastern Russia, this small sea duck comes to breed.
It hides its nest well, on the ground beside a stream.
Its feathers lie smooth and packed tight, trapping a store of air.
Young birds start courting in their earliest winter, yet a male rarely keeps a lasting mate before his fourth.
Once paired, they may stay together for years, though fathers rarely help with the young.

tagline.text: Feathers packed with air, nest hidden by the rushing stream.

facts.text: The Caspian tern is the world's largest species of tern, with a subcosmopolitan but scattered distribution.
They feed mainly on fish, which they dive for, hovering high over the water and then plunging.
Breeding is in spring and summer, with one to three pale blue-green eggs, with heavy brown spotting, being laid.
The call is a loud heron-like croak.
They may fly up to 60 km from the breeding colony to catch fish; they often fish on freshwater lakes as well as at sea.
They nest either together in colonies, or singly in mixed colonies of other tern and gull species.
Their breeding habitat is large lakes and ocean coasts in North America, and locally in Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australasia.
North American birds migrate to southern coasts, the West Indies and northernmost South America.
Its wingspan is about 128 cm.
It weighs about 655 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Over a wide lake comes a loud croak, like a heron's, from the largest tern in the world.
It hovers high above the water, then plunges down for a fish.
For a meal it may fly up to 60 kilometres from its colony, to lakes or out to sea.
In spring and summer it lays pale blue-green eggs, heavily spotted with brown.
Some nest in crowds of their own kind; others nest alone among gulls and other terns.

tagline.text: The biggest tern of all, croaking like a heron.

facts.text: The varied thrush is a member of the thrush family, Turdidae.
The varied thrush is predominantly insectivorous, though its diet varies throughout the course of the year.
The breeding habitat is dense coniferous forest, with two to five eggs being laid in a tree nest.
Nests in Alaska, Yukon Territory, and mountains in Alberta, British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon.
Young varied thrushes are generally brown, though their stomach feathers are white, and initially harbor two orange stripes at the covert feathers.
During the summer, ground-dwelling arthropods make up the bulk of its diet.
Seen in flocks during winter of up to 20 birds.
Eggs are generally 3–4 per nest, but sometimes 2–5.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 36 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 78 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It lays 3 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Deep in dense coniferous forest, from Alaska and the Yukon down the mountains to Oregon, this member of the thrush family comes to breed.
In summer it hunts the forest floor, where ground-dwelling arthropods make up most of its meals.
Mostly it eats insects, yet its diet shifts as the year turns, and so, the tale says, it earned its name.
In winter it gathers in flocks of up to 20 birds.

tagline.text: A forest hunter whose table changes with the year.

facts.text: The dark-eyed junco is a species of junco, a group of small, grayish New World sparrows.
They mainly eat seeds and insects, with seeds comprising three quarters of their year-round diet.
Dark-eyed juncos usually nest in a cup-shaped depression on the ground, well-hidden by vegetation or other material, although nests are sometimes found in the lower branches of a shrub or tree.
In winter, dark-eyed juncos are familiar in and around towns, and in many places are the most common birds at feeders.
The song is a trill similar to the chipping sparrow's, except that the red-backed dark-eyed junco's song is more complex, similar to that of the yellow-eyed junco.
Young dark-eyed juncos also depend on a diet of mainly insects.
Normally, two clutches of four eggs are laid during the breeding season.
The call also resembles that of the black-throated blue warbler which is a member of the New World warbler family.
Its wingspan is about 25 cm.
It weighs about 20 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a burrow, a crevice, an old nest another bird built or a cup.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: In winter, the dark-eyed junco keeps close to towns, and at many feeders it is the most common bird of all.
This small, grayish New World sparrow eats mostly seeds, yet its young grow up on insects.
Its song is a trill, much like a chipping sparrow's.
In the breeding season it tucks a cup-shaped nest into a hollow on the ground, well hidden by plants, and normally lays two clutches of eggs.

tagline.text: The small gray sparrow that crowds the winter feeder

facts.text: The short-billed gull is a species of gull that breeds in northwestern North America.
The short-billed gull breeds in colonies along coastal areas and inland wetlands, mainly in Alaska and Northwest Canada.
Its wings appear long and narrow in flight relative to its short body.
In North America, it was previously known as the mew gull, when it was considered conspecific with the palearctic common gull.
It is a very rare visitor to eastern North America and a vagrant to east Asia.
In breeding plumage, adults have a white head, pale eyes surrounded by a red orbital skin, yellow legs and bill with no markings.
The species was first described by Scottish naturalist John Richardson in 1831 as the 'short-billed mew gull', Larus brachyrhynchus.

Though some authorities, including the American Ornithologist's Union from 1931 onwards, have long considered brachyrhynchus to be a subspecies of the common gull, others have recognized the two as distinct species.
Its wingspan is about 110 cm.
It weighs about 412 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in coasts.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 1 to 5 eggs in a clutch.

sentences.text: On the coasts and inland wetlands of Alaska and northwest Canada, it breeds in colonies, its nest a cup.
Then it wears a white head, a plain yellow bill, and pale eyes ringed in red.
Its wings look long and narrow against its short body.
It travels between breeding and wintering grounds, and a rare few stray to eastern North America or east Asia.
Once it shared the name mew gull with the common gull.

tagline.text: A wanderer with narrow wings and a once-shared name.

facts.text: The California gull is a medium-sized gull, smaller on average than the herring gull, but larger on average than the ring-billed gull.
They mainly eat insects, fish and the eggs and young of other birds, especially ducklings.
The breeding habitat of the California gull are lakes and marshes in interior western North America from the Northwest Territories, Canada south to eastern California and Colorado.
Opportunistic feeders, California gulls often can be seen scavenging at garbage dumps, marinas and docks.
They nest in colonies, sometimes with other birds.
A monument in Salt Lake City commemorates this event, known as the "Miracle of the Gulls".
In California, the California gull at one time held the protected status California Species of Special Concern due to declining numbers at their historic California breeding colony at Mono Lake.
The California gull is the state bird of Utah, remembered for assisting Mormon settlers in dealing with a plague of Mormon crickets.
Its wingspan is about 121 cm.
It weighs about 683 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in coasts.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Inland, among the lakes and marshes of western North America, the California gull raises its young in crowded colonies, sometimes beside other birds.
It feeds on insects, fish, and the eggs and young of other birds, and it will scavenge at garbage dumps, marinas and docks.
Utah made it the state bird, remembering how it helped Mormon settlers face a plague of Mormon crickets.
In Salt Lake City, a monument honors that event, known as the Miracle of the Gulls.

tagline.text: The gull Utah remembers for the Miracle of the Gulls.

facts.text: The ring-billed gull is a medium-sized gull native to North America, breeding in Canada and the northern Contiguous United States, and wintering mainly in the United States and northern Mexico.
Ring-billed gulls forage in flight or pick up objects while swimming, walking or wading.
They nest colonially on the ground, often on islands, but also increasingly on flat factory roofs.
In the late 19th century, the ring-billed gull was hunted for its plumage.
They are omnivorous; their diet may include insects, fish, grain, eggs, earthworms and rodents.
The specific delawarensis refers to the Delaware River.
The breeding habitat is near lakes, rivers, or the coast across most of Canada, and the northern United States.
The total population was estimated as 2.55 million birds in 2006, and still in 2018.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 120 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 516 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in coasts.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 3 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Look to the islands, and to the flat roofs of factories: there the ring-billed gull nests in colonies, close beside its neighbors.
Its name carries a river, the Delaware, though it breeds by lakes, rivers and coasts across Canada and the northern United States.
It snatches food in flight, or picks it up while swimming, walking or wading.
Insects, fish, grain, eggs, earthworms, rodents: this gull turns away very little.

tagline.text: Hatched on islands and factory roofs, fed on almost anything.

facts.text: The glaucous-winged gull is a large, white-headed gull.
The glaucous-winged gull nests in the summer, and each pair produces two or three chicks which fledge at six weeks.
The longevity record, though, is more than 37 years, for a bird banded as a chick in British Columbia.
Young birds are brown or gray with black beaks, and take four years to reach adult plumage.
It feeds along the coast, scavenging for dead or weak animals, fish, mussels and scraps.
It is a resident from the western coast of Alaska to the coast of Washington.
It has a white head, neck, breast, and belly, a white tail.
The specific glaucescens is Neo-Latin for "glaucous" from the Ancient Greek, glaukos, denoting the grey color of its wings.
Its wingspan is about 146 cm.
It weighs about 1.1 kg.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in coasts.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It lays 1 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Along the coast from western Alaska down to Washington, a large white-headed bird keeps its home all year.
It works the shoreline, scavenging for dead or weak animals, fish, mussels and scraps.
In summer each pair raises a small brood of young, dressed in brown or gray with black beaks.
They wait years to earn the white head and belly of their elders.
One, banded as a chick in British Columbia, lived more than 37 years.

tagline.text: A white-headed scavenger who works the coast all year.

facts.text: Heermann's gull is a gull resident in the United States, Mexico and extreme southwestern British Columbia, nearly all nesting on Isla Rasa in the Gulf of California.
Heermann's gull eats small fish, marine invertebrates, lizards, insects, and carrion.
After the islands eroded away by 2007, the colony continued to nest on nearby rooftops.
Egg-collecting and disturbance during the breeding season are discouraged.
The nests are often at densities as high as 110 nests per 100 m2.
In June 2018, one of the colony's main nesting sites, the Seaside McDonald's, was destroyed by a drunk driving crash.
The success of the colony in any one year is dependent on the availability of prey and this is related to the ocean temperature changes brought about by El Niño.
They are usually found near shores or well out to sea, very rarely inland.
Its wingspan is about 114 cm.

It lives mostly in coasts.

The IUCN Red List rates it Near Threatened.

sentences.text: On Isla Rasa, in the Gulf of California, nearly all Heermann's gulls gather to nest.
There the nests crowd so close that one small patch of ground can hold over a hundred.
Each year the colony's luck rides on its prey, which comes and goes with the ocean changes of El Niño.
Where its islands wore away, a colony moved to nearby rooftops, though one of them, a Seaside McDonald's, was wrecked by a drunk driver's crash.

tagline.text: When the islands wear away, the rooftops will do.

facts.text: The orange-crowned warbler is a small songbird of the New World warbler family.
They forage actively in low shrubs, flying from perch to perch, sometimes hovering.
The nest is a small open cup well-concealed on the ground under vegetation or low in shrubs.
The song of is a trill, descending in pitch and volume.
The female builds the nest; four to six eggs are laid in a nest on the ground or in a low bush.
The call is a high chip.
The type locality is Omaha, Nebraska.
Their breeding habitat is open shrubby areas across Canada, Alaska and the western United States.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 19 cm from its wing length.

It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.

sentences.text: Across the open shrubby country of Canada, Alaska and the western United States, the little orange-crowned warbler works the low shrubs, flitting from perch to perch and sometimes hovering in the air.
Its song is a trill that tumbles down, falling lower and softer as it goes, and its call is a high chip.
When nesting comes, the female builds a small open cup, well hidden on the ground under plants or low in a bush.

tagline.text: A falling trill from the low shrubs.

facts.text: The long-billed dowitcher is a medium-sized shorebird with a relatively long bill belonging to the sandpiper family, Scolopacidae.
They feed in various freshwater habitats with their bill underwater in a "sewing machine" motion and have a mating display where males chase females in flight.
The long-billed dowitcher, during breeding, consumes large quantities of chironomidae larva and larva of other insects with occasional plant matter and seeds.
Male long-billed dowitcher will court females by first singing to them and then compete with other males by pursuing the female in flight, displaying an aerial show of speed and agility.
The long-billed dowitcher's main call, mostly heard in flight but also while on ground, is a high, sharp keek sometimes repeated as an accelerating quick double or triple note series.
Between the two, the best distinguishing field mark is their flight call, especially in winter, when the two species' plumage can be nearly identical.
Dowitchers eat everything from polychaetes to insect larva to crustaceans to mollusks.
After mating, they are known to sing while hovering 15 feet in the air above their territories.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 48 cm from its wing length.

It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 3 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Near Threatened.

sentences.text: In fresh water, bill under the surface, it stitches up and down like a sewing machine.
When breeding, it gathers midge larvae in great numbers, with now and then a seed.
Come courting, a male sings, then races rival males after a female through the air.
After mating, he hovers fifteen feet above his territory and sings again.
In winter, when it looks like its kin, its high, sharp keek in flight tells it apart.

tagline.text: Stitching the water, singing in the sky.

facts.text: The hooded merganser is a species of fish-eating duck in the subfamily Anatinae.
The hooded merganser is a diving predator that largely hunts by sight while under water.
Males and females of the hooded merganser form monogamous pairs and they remain together until the female has selected a nesting cavity and completed laying her clutch.
Because these waterfowl are cavity nesters, they require mature trees in which cavities have been excavated, however, they also will use nest boxes supplied by humans.
Females will actively seek out cavities in dead trees or artificial nest boxes such as those provided for nesting wood ducks.
Hooded mergansers are short-distance migrants, and they winter in the United States in regions where winter temperatures allow for ice-free conditions on ponds, lakes and rivers.
One is in the eastern United States from the southern Canada–US border along the Atlantic Coast to the Gulf Coast in the region of the Mississippi delta.
The bird is striking in appearance; both sexes have crests that they can raise or lower, and the breeding plumage of the male is handsomely patterned and colored.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 65 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 614 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It nests in a cavity.
It lays 6 to 18 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Under the water, the hooded merganser hunts by sight, a diving duck that lives on fish.
On the surface, both sexes can raise or lower their crests.
Mates keep together only until she has chosen a hollow and laid her full clutch.
She seeks that hollow in dead trees, or in nest boxes people set out for wood ducks.
In winter they travel only a short way, to ponds, lakes and rivers free of ice.

tagline.text: A crested hunter that dives and finds its fish by sight.

facts.text: The red crossbill or common crossbill is a small passerine bird in the finch family Fringillidae.
Crossbills have distinctive mandibles, crossed at the tips, which enable them to extract seeds from conifer cones and other fruits.
Its movements and occurrence are linked very closely to the availability of conifer seeds, its primary food source.
While each type may be seen to feed on many different conifer species when not breeding, each has optimal breeding success only in a particular type of conifer forest.
Using their crossed mandibles for leverage, crossbills are able to efficiently separate the scales of conifer cones and extract the seeds on which they feed.
They typically nest in late summer when the seeds of most conifer species mature, but may nest at any time of year if they locate an area with a suitable cone crop.
Birds of all types are essentially identical in appearance but have slight differences in their calls and songs.
Crossbills are distinguished by the mandibles crossing at their tips, which gives the group its English name.
Its wingspan is about 30 cm.
It weighs about 38 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in forest.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: In the conifer forest, a small finch works a cone with a beak whose tips cross.
Using that cross for leverage, it pries the scales apart and draws out its chief food, the seeds.
Where the seeds go, it goes, for its wanderings are tied to the cone crops.
It nests mostly in late summer, when the seeds ripen, yet may nest in any season where cones are plenty.
Its kinds look alike, differing only slightly in calls and songs.

tagline.text: Where the cone seeds go, it follows.

facts.text: The American wigeon, also known as the baldpate, is a species of dabbling duck found in North America.
Wigeons also commonly feed on dry land, eating waste grain in harvested fields and grazing on pasture grasses, winter wheat, clover, and lettuce.
The nest is a depression on dry ground, often some distance from water.
She nests on the ground, near water and under cover, and lays 6–12 creamy white eggs.
